groups.text: flatMap takes a function that returns a publisher, called the inner, like this Mono from a fraud service.
For each id, flatMap subscribes to the inner right away, without waiting for earlier ones to finish.
Three ids arrive together: three, one and two.
Id three takes three hundred milliseconds to score, id one takes one hundred, and id two takes two hundred.
flatMap subscribes to all three at time zero, so the three calls run at the same time.
Call one finishes first, and flatMap passes it on at once.
Then two, then three.
The output is one, two, three.
flatMap merges results in the order they arrive, not in input order, and everything is done at three hundred milliseconds.
flatMap creates no threads.
These calls overlap only because each inner is asynchronous, like a non-blocking HTTP call.
By default, up to two hundred fifty-six inners run at once.
When the calls hit a shared service, pass a limit, such as four.
The limit is also its demand.
flatMap asks the source for four ids, then for one more each time a call finishes.
When order matters, concatMap subscribes to one inner at a time.
It asks for the next id only when the current inner completes.
three runs first, for three hundred milliseconds.
Then one, then two.
Input order: three, one, two.
But the times add up, so it is done at six hundred milliseconds.
flatMapSequential subscribes to all three at once, like flatMap, but it hands the results on in input order.
one and two finish early, so they wait in a buffer.
When three finishes, all three go out, in order.
Input order, and done at three hundred milliseconds.
The price is memory for the buffer, and one slow first call holds back everything behind it.
Same input, three operators.
Use concatMap when each call must wait for the previous one, like postings to one ledger account.
Kotlin Flow starts from the other side.
It is sequential by default, like concatMap.
You opt in to overlap with flatMapMerge, and Flow has no flatMapSequential.
